records.name: Opening tableau

source_blocks.text: Trigger: New game

Late afternoon in Civeton. Children use carved wooden monster figures and sticks to imitate adult trainers and crusaders. Pate declares that he and Trade are righteous champions of the True Light. Aimon is assigned the Dawn Bloom defenders because he is the youngest and because someone has to be the ‘enemy’. Nothing about the boys’ behaviour suggests personal hatred; the language is inherited play.

Environmental NPC snippets should show adults treating the coming crusade as history repeating itself: old veterans, shrine stories, and parents using phrases the children later mimic without understanding them.

records.name: Pretend battle tutorial

source_blocks.text: Teach basic turn selection, type readability and HP with toy/imaginary monsters. At 0 HP the imaginary monster dramatically ‘falls’ and the children argue about whether the move was fair. No death language is used.
Pate plays aggressively; Trade interrupts to clarify rules. Aimon is outnumbered but praised for improvising.
Battle: Scripted tutorial; no persistent team state

records.name: The fall

source_blocks.text: During the game Aimon slips or is knocked over. Pate instantly drops the crusader performance and helps him up. Trade checks his hands/knees and scolds Pate for playing too hard. The thematic image is simple: ideology vanishes the moment a real person is hurt.
Pate promises Aimon that when he is older he will come with them. Trade adds, ‘If you’re ready.’ Pate answers that of course he will be.

records.name: Morning of departure

source_blocks.text: Trigger: prologue_complete

Years later. Aimon wakes to bells, flags and an unusually busy village. The crusade has formally begun. NPCs are excited, frightened or proud. The tone intentionally resembles the start of a conventional heroic RPG.
The player is free to revisit the childhood play site. The hill feels smaller now.

source_blocks.text: At Pate’s home Aimon learns he departed before dawn after claiming a real monster. His family assumed Aimon had been told. A small personal item or unfinished breakfast reinforces the speed of departure.

source_blocks.text: Trade is gone too. Aimon finds a brief note: ‘Don’t follow us.’ It reads as an order because Trade writes concisely. Later context will reveal it was protection, not rejection.
Aimon is angry rather than tearful. His immediate goal becomes catching them.

records.name: Kurg refuses

source_blocks.text: At the mustering camp, General Kurg Halbrecht refuses Aimon without ceremony. After repeated insistence, Kurg reveals that Pate and Trade specifically asked him not to enlist Aimon. Kurg says they were trying to keep him alive.
Aimon interprets this as proof they still think he is weak. He states that he will follow them with or without permission. Kurg believes him.

source_blocks.text: Kurg authorises supervised enlistment rather than letting Aimon travel alone. Three starter species are presented. The player chooses one. The two remaining starters are assigned dynamically to Pate and Trade, with personality-preferred mapping used when both mappings are possible.
This is a genuine emotional milestone: Aimon believes he is finally becoming the kind of person Pate and Trade thought he was not ready to be.

source_blocks.text: A camp trainer tests Aimon. Before battle, Kurg explains that genuine combat has no magical fainting convention: if a monster is pushed to 0 HP, it dies. This test therefore uses formal surrender thresholds and a referee.
The player is taught that story battles can end by surrender before lethal damage, while wilderness/hostile combat can be permanent.

records.name: Departure

source_blocks.text: Aimon leaves Civeton with the marching road ahead. Kurg’s final instruction is practical, not inspirational: stay alive, learn before committing, report when possible. Aimon’s own private objective remains Pate and Trade.

ACT II — THE CRUSADE

Eight settlements form the mortal-world spine. Each chapter repeats a legible gameplay rhythm — arrive, explore, trace Pate/Trade, resolve local crisis, defeat leader, choose spare/execute, revisit changed town — while the moral context changes beneath that familiar structure. The repeated form is deliberate: the player’s mechanics remain stable while their interpretation of those mechanics changes.

records.name: Border road ambush

source_blocks.text: A Dawn Bloom patrol attacks the True Light column after warnings are ignored. The fight is clearly military and reciprocal, allowing Aimon to read the conflict as straightforward defence versus invasion depending on perspective.
Rhoswen praises decisive action. Aeric tends wounded from both sides if the player remains nearby.
Battle: First lethal hostile-trainer encounter

source_blocks.text: Aimon reaches a keep controlling the road. True Light soldiers have not breached it. Kurg authorises Aimon to seek a formal monster challenge against commander Ser Aldren March to avoid a larger assault.

source_blocks.text: Aldren accepts because losing one formal battle is preferable to losing the keep and civilians in a siege. He is stern and hostile but honours surrender rules. His team is disciplined and direct.

The battle is defensive and restorative, making the player work to overcome endurance rather than aggression.

source_blocks.text: Provost Corvin Sair receives Aimon politely and offers to transfer control in exchange for protection of his commercial privileges. This is the first leader who seems more interested in office than faith.

source_blocks.text: Optional investigation chain follows false invoices, warehouse seals and displaced families being charged extortionate prices. Evidence proves Corvin and True Light intermediaries both profited. The corruption is cross-factional, not a Dawn Bloom-only vice.
Completing the chain lets the post-conquest administration break the network; ignoring it means the True Light occupation inherits it intact.

source_blocks.text: Instead of an immediate challenge, Samiel asks Aimon to walk through the town. This sequence is interactive: children play, farmers work, families pray, and monster partners help in orchards. The point is visual sameness with Civeton rather than exposition.
Samiel does not ask Aimon to convert or defect. He asks what Aimon believes the war is for.

records.name: The same story

source_blocks.text: At the shrine Samiel compares creation narratives. Both religions describe darkness before first light, a radiant presence, and a moral duty to guide the lost. Names, ritual gestures and later commentaries differ; foundational images are nearly identical.
Samiel asks: ‘If your light teaches mercy and mine teaches mercy, what exactly are we killing one another over?’ Aimon has no answer.

This short act lets grief breathe before the supernatural pivot. Aimon tries normal responses first. Severin’s offer therefore feels like a genuine violation of the world rather than an obvious next quest marker.

source_blocks.text: Severin explains that death is initially a transition of identity into the underworld. For a limited period, a coherent human self remains retrievable. Eventually identity passes beyond a boundary that cannot be reversed. Pate and Trade died recently enough that a window remains.
This is not general resurrection. Success requires physically entering the underworld, reaching the held souls, overcoming its ruler and returning before dissolution.

ACT IV — DESCENT

The Nine Circles are human names for regions of the underworld. They are not divinely designed punishments for a Christian-style list of sins. Humans imposed moral categories on natural/metaphysical processes they did not understand. Each chapter nonetheless mirrors an emotional or institutional problem Aimon has encountered, because human dead reshape local space through memory and fixation.

ACT V — NO GODS, NO MASTERS

The finale must not reveal an evil god behind the war. The cosmic beings are indifferent, and that is more devastating. Human institutions created the conflict and therefore humans retain responsibility for ending it.

The emotional beat is not mockery. Illyr treats the issue with the mild attention one might give an unexpected pattern in insects.

He states, in his own simple voice, that they do not get to decide what is right for him merely because they are greater.

Kurg eventually begins ceasefire negotiations because he chooses to, not because Aimon or Illyr commands him.

source_blocks.text: Aimon reaches the final court and finds Severin on Nharos’s former throne in an evolved poet-king form. He does not deny using Aimon. He points out that he promised to lead Aimon to his friends and did exactly that.

records.name: Why rule?

source_blocks.text: Severin’s justification is practical and philosophically dangerous: the underworld requires coordination, old authority proved vulnerable, and he understood the system better than anyone positioned to replace it. Aimon asks whether challenging authority was merely Severin’s route to becoming authority.
Severin considers that a fair question rather than an accusation he must dodge.

source_blocks.text: Severin wants to test the person who defeated gods and unknowingly made a king. His team is built around system mastery: control, prediction, efficient use of one apparently ordinary species, and a thematic ace.

records.name: After victory

source_blocks.text: Aimon defeats Severin but does not automatically depose him. Severin yields the contest, amused. Aimon has no desire to rule the dead and no evidence that removing Severin would improve anything.
